paper_title: Cross-modal Steering Vectors Exist Across Both Image and Text Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Are concepts and mechanisms unified across modalities in current AI models, or instead implemented separately for each one? We operationalize this broad question of modality unification by studying cross-modal steering: 1) finding vectors that successfully steer generation on tokens of one modality, which then 2) transfer zero-shot to steer generation when added to tokens of another modality. Our study goes beyond simple correlational alignment (e.g. representational similarity) because steering is fundamentally causal. We study cross-modal steering in several unified multimodal models (UMMs), since they possess shared parameters for language and image generation, focusing on these two modalities. Across diverse steered concepts such as emotion and object size, we show that steering vectors transfer zero-shot in both directions (text-to-image & image-to-text). Even for concepts that are highly unique to one modality (e.g. formal vs. colloquial language), steering vectors often induce a consistent, interpretable effect in the other modality, such as formal clothing and design. This transfer has a geometric signature too: despite a clear modality gap separating text and image representations, steering vectors with strong cross-modal transferability tend to point in similar directions for the same concept. Our findings shed light on how vision and language interact inside unified multimodal models and point towards more general, modality-agnostic approaches for controlling their behavior.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Despite the complexity of modern generative models, such as LLMs and diffusion models, many high-level concepts can be controlled through surprisingly simple interventions: adding linear direction, or steering vector (Subramani et al., 2022), to models intermediate representations. Steering vectors have been used to modulate wide range of behaviors in both language models (Li et al., 2023; Todd et al., 2024; Turner et al., 2024; Dunefsky & Cohan, 2025; Bayat et al., 2025) and image generation systems (Bau et al., 2019; Goetschalckx et al., 2019; Spingarn et al., 2021; Park et al., 2023; Gandikota et al., 2024; Konovalova et al., 2026), providing lightweight and causal means of controlling model outputs. Yet steering in these two modalities has largely been studied separately. Here we ask: are steering directions themselves modality-specific, or can direction discovered in one modality also control generation in another? Consider steering vector extracted entirely from text that, when added to models hidden states, reliably causes it to write more formally. If the same model also generates images, what happens when that very same vector is instead added to its generated image tokens? Could it induce corresponding notion of visual formality, such as more formal clothing or design? And vice versa: could direction extracted purely from images steer how the model writes? We call this cross-modal steering, illustrated in Figure 1, and ask: Can steering vector constructed only on tokens from one modality generalize zero-shot when added to tokens from the other modality? This question connects to broader debate about how concepts are represented across modalities. On the one hand, recent evidence from multimodal models suggests substantial internal separaWork done primarily at Mila, McGill University. Correspondence to bkrojer@northeastern.edu. 1 Preprint. Under review. Figure 1: Cross-modal steering vectors transfer zero-shot in both directions. steering vector extracted entirely from one modality can steer generation both within that modality and, without any adaptation, in the other. tion between language and vision: text and image token representations remain nearly orthogonal throughout the layers (Serra et al., 2025), knowledge edited on the text side mostly fails to show up in generated images (Gao et al., 2026), and circuits in multi-modal LLMs for the same task are often disjoint (Nikankin et al., 2025). On the other hand, cognitive science has long proposed modality-agnostic semantic hub where concepts live regardless of whether they arrive through language or perception (Patterson et al., 2007). We investigate this through cross-modal steering: successful transfer would demonstrate that common direction causally modulates concept across modalities, even when their representations may occupy distinct regions in activation space. In the mainstream paradigms of multimodal modeling (Rombach et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024), it would not be possible to answer this question since image-to-text and text-to-image generation are separately parameterized and modeled either via autoregression (Radford et al., 2019) or diffusion (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015). Thus, we turn to unified multimodal models (UMMs) as natural testbed for cross-modal steering (Wang et al., 2026b; Team, 2025; Zhou et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Jiao et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2025). Some frontier proprietary systems have similarly moved to generating images natively within shared language-model architecture rather than calling separate image model (Gemini Team, 2023; OpenAI, 2025). Yet shared parameters do not imply shared internal mechanisms, making cross-modal transfer far from guaranteed. Indeed, prior work studying cross-modal steering in UMMs reports strong asymmetry: text-derived vectors transfer well to image generation, but image-derived vectors struggle to transfer to text generation including limited transfer in autoregressive models (Wang & Li, 2026). We find that steering vectors transfer across modalities in both directions. We tested three UMMs that autoregressively generate text and image tokens from shared weight space: UniAR (Peng et al., 2026), Emu3.5 (Cui et al., 2025) and Liquid (Wu et al., 2026). In UniAR, the transferred vector is almost as good as the intra-modality vector for steering, recovering 84% of its steering effect on images and 74% on text. In Emu3.5 and Liquid, text-derived vectors sometimes even steer images better than image-derived ones. This illustrates the promise of studying cross-modal steering: steering vector can be constructed in whichever modality is easier, and then used in the other. This matters most for concepts that are highly unique to one modality (see Figure 1). How such vector would express itself in the other modality gives glimpse of how the model bridges vision and language: steering an image generator with vector for formal vs. colloquial language causes people or rooms to be depicted more formally, and steering language model with vector for low image resolution causes the model to write shorter text and express uncertainty. Finally, we show that cross-modal steering has geometric signature: despite clear modality gap between text 2 Preprint. Under review. and image representations, the text and image vectors of many concepts point in similar directions. The closer they are, the better they facilitate transfer (3.4). Together, our results show that modality-specific representations can nevertheless contain shared causal directions of control, revealing form of internal structure that is neither fully modalityspecific nor captured simply by representational alignment. Beyond offering new lens on how vision and language interact inside unified models, cross-modal steering points toward modalityagnostic approaches for controlling multimodal generation.

sections.title: 2.1 PRELIMINARIES
sections.content: Unified Multimodal Models. In our study, we consider unified multimodal models (UMMs) that generate both language and visual content in one autoregressive stream, from an underlying shared weight space (Wang et al., 2026b; Team, 2025; Cui et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026; Peng et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). Concretely, UMM models mixed sequence = (x1, . . . , xT ), in which every token xt is either text token or discrete visual token, with single next-token objective: pθ(x) = (cid:89) t=1 pθ(xt x<t) , where the parameters θ are shared across modalities, The term unified is used broadly in the literature, and can even include models with mostly separate parameters and mixed objectives (Deng et al., 2025). For our study, we require models to share the weights responsible for generation. shared autoregressive objective additionally lets us extract and apply steering vectors in the same manner on both token types. We study three such UMMs: UniAR (8B) (Peng et al., 2026), Emu3.5 (34B) (Cui et al., 2025) and Liquid (7B) (Wu et al., 2026). They differ most in how images are tokenized: UniARs image tokens are semantic, derived from language-aligned vision encoder, whereas those of Emu3.5 and Liquid are trained to reconstruct pixels. Steering Vectors. Steering is any intervention on model internals that allows continuous modulation of the output generation or behavior by adding vector to the intermediate hidden states during generation (Subramani et al., 2019; 2022; Li et al., 2023; Turner et al., 2024): = hl + α vl. Here hl is hidden representation at layer l, vl is the steering vector, and the scalar α sets the strength and sign of the intervention. The two key design choices are a) how to find such vector and b) how to apply it during generation. In LLMs, steering vectors are typically found from contrastive prompt pairs or from probes and sparse dictionaries trained on the residual stream, and applied to one or many layers at every step of token-by-token decoding (Li et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024; Huben et al., 2024). In image generation, directions are instead often discovered in the latent space of diffusion model (e.g., by unsupervised decomposition) or learned as lightweight adapters, and applied along the denoising trajectory (Kwon et al., 2023; Park et al., 2023; Haas et al., 2024; Gandikota et al., 2024). The contrastive recipe that is standard for LLMs is less common in vision (Haas et al., 2024; Gaintseva et al., 2026; Konovalova et al., 2026), in part because minimal image pairs are much harder to curate than minimal text pairs.

sections.title: 2.2 OUR APPROACH
sections.content: We adopt one established approach for both language and vision: we find steering vectors via dataset of minimally different inputs, and add them to representations at either subset of layers or whole ranges of layers. Crucially, finding and applying the vector need not use the same modality: for cross-modal steering, we construct vector entirely from examples in one modality and then apply that same vector, without any adaptation or target-modality data, to representations of the other modality during generation. This gives four steering settings, corresponding to all combinations of finding vector in either modality and applying it to either modality, as illustrated in Figure 1. Throughout the paper, we refer to them as txttxt, txtimg, imgtxt, and imgimg: txtimg and imgtxt are the transfer settings we primarily study, and the intra-modality settings txttxt and imgimg serve as reference points. sections.title: 3.1 MEASURING CROSS-MODAL TRANSFER
sections.content: Given concept c, steering strength α and an evaluation prompt p, we write xc,α,p for the steered output and xp for the unsteered output at α = 0. We measure steering success with an LLM judge that compares the two, and further quantify cross-modal transfer by comparing how well transferred vector steers with how well the intra-modality vector does. Concept rate. We use Gemini 3.7 Flash (Google DeepMind, 2026) as the judge. It sees xp and xc,α,p in random order, without knowing which one is steered, and is asked which one shows more of pole of the concept, for example happy for emotion, with the asked pole chosen at random between the concepts two poles. The correct answer is the steered output when the judge is asked for the pole that α steers toward, and the baseline otherwise. We score each pair (xp, xc,α,p) as J(xp, xc,α,p) = (cid:26)1, 0, if the judge picks the correct output, if it picks the other output or answers Tie. The concept rate is the mean score over the 20 prompts of concept, CRc,α = 1 (cid:88) pP J(xp, xc,α,p) , = 20. To summarize concept-rate curve across steering strengths α with one number, we take its normalized area under the curve, AUCc [0, 1]. An AUC of 1 means the judge identified the concept in every output at every strength, and 0 that it never did. 3 Cross-modal recovery. To judge transfer, we measure how much of the intra-modality steering performance (i.e., AUCc) transferred vector recovers. We consider the intra-modality vector as reference point since we expect vector to steer the modality it was found in best. Thus recovery is defined for image generation as Recimg and for text generation as Rectxt: AUCc(txt img) AUCc(img img) AUCc(img txt) AUCc(txt txt) Recimg = Rectxt = , . recovery of 1 means the transferred vector steers as well as the intra-modality one, 0 means it does not steer at all, and above 1 means it steers better. Since each setting has its own strength range (2.2), recovery compares each vector over the strength ranges it tolerates, not at equal α. Further details. The judge agrees with human raters at Cohens κ = 0.62 (Cohen, 1960). On top of concept rate, we separately report metric for output quality, namely the fluency of steered text and the visual quality of steered images, adopted from (Wu et al., 2025b). sections.title: 3.2 RESULTS
sections.content: Across our three models and eight concepts, we report Cross-modal Recovery (both Recimg and Rectxt) in Figure 3 and table 1. The concept-rate curves underlying these numbers are shown in Figure 2 for UniAR and in the Appendix for Emu3.5 and Liquid (Figures 11 and 12). Steering vectors transfer in both directions. In all three models, vectors found in one modality also steer generation in the other for most concepts (Figure 3 and table 1). For every concept except spatial, there is layer range at which text-derived vectors recover more than 80% of the intramodality effect, in all three models. UniAR exhibits the strongest cross-modal steering effects: at middle layers, transferred vectors recover on average 84% of the intra-modality effect on images and 74% on text, and its concept-rate curves in Figure 2 follow the intra-modality curves closely for most concepts.4 txtimg is strongest at middle layers in all three models; transfer into text peaks at early layers in UniAR and at late layers in Emu3.5 and Liquid, where their mean imgtxt recovery reaches 0.87 and 0.91. Examples for txtimg and imgtxt are shown in Figure 4. 3AUC measures are commonly used as summary statistics in machine learning (e.g. for benchmark evaluation (Subramani et al., 2025b), classification (AUROC; Marcum, 1960), and calibration (El-Yaniv & Wiener, 2010; Subramani et al., 2025a; 2026), and in the sciences (Wagner & Ayres, 1977; Hanley & McNeil, 1982). 4We speculate this is due to the difference in image encoders (see 2.2). 5 Preprint. Concept rate is the fraction of steered outputs in which an LLM judge finds the concept shifted toward the steered pole (3.1), plotted against normalized steering strength. Black curves show intra-modality steering (top: imgimg, bottom: txttxt). The colored areas indicate the gap between the two, either when transfer performs better (green) or worse (red). Recovery in Figure 3 and table 1 quantifies this comparison. For most concepts, the transfer curve comes close to the intra-modality curve. txtimg is easier than imgtxt. Text-derived vectors steer images for nearly every concept, and in Emu3.5 and Liquid even often better than intra-modality steering (imgimg): their txtimg recovery averages 1.10 and 1.20, i.e., above 1. We hypothesize this is mostly due to weaker imagederived vectors in these two models rather than particularly strong transfer: imgimg reaches an AUC of only 0.44 and 0.43 at middle layers, compared to 0.83 in UniAR. Practically, for these two models, text vectors are the better vectors for steering images, despite image-derived vectors being native to the space. In the other direction, imgtxt is only widely successful in UniAR, while more mixed in Emu3.5 and Liquid. UniAR recovers on average up to 0.96 of the intra-modality effect, whereas Emu3.5 and Liquid come close only at late layers (0.87 and 0.91). Emotion transfers best, size and spatial worst. Emotion transfers most evenly, with mean recovery of 0.95 in both directions, and age transfers into images better than other concepts (1.02 1.87 across models and layer ranges). Visual concepts tend to work better in the txtimg setting than in imgtxt. Size shows this most clearly with overall mean recovery of 1.12 for txtimg but only 0.32 for imgtxt. The only concept that fails across most settings is spatial (left-right), with moderate success only for imgimg in UniAR (see curve in Figure 2) and minor effects for txttxt in Emu3.5 and Liquid. Output quality. We check whether there is strong trade-off between high concept rates and output quality. With an AxBench-like judge (Wu et al., 2025b), we find that output quality noticeably drops only beyond the strengths where the concept rate plateaus (and, for text, then drops): at 0.4 of the strength range, where the text concept rate peaks, text fluency is still at about three quarters of the level of unsteered outputs, and it collapses beyond that point (Appendix A.7). On the image generation side the trade-off is smaller: image coherence is still at about 90% of its unsteered level at 0.6 of the range, where the concept rate has already reached over 90% of its maximum.

sections.title: 3.4 GEOMETRY OF STEERING VECTORS
sections.content: Do text-derived and image-derived steering vectors point in similar directions? And if that is the case, would their cosine similarity be predictive how well cross-modal steering works? Finding: Cosine similarities correlate with cross-modal steering (Figure 5). For UniAR and Liquid, we find that cosine similarities for most concepts are significantly above zero6, up to 0.60 (UniAR) and 0.51 (Liquid). On the other hand, Emu3.5s steering vectors are close to zero cosine similarity for all concepts except color (maximum 0.24). Concretely, averaging across all (model, concept, layer range) points, we find moderate correlation between cosine similarity and our main metric of steering transfer (recovery, averaged over both transfer directions): Spearman ρ = 0.38 (p < 0.01), Pearson = 0.22 (n = 63, the 21 points per model of Figure 5). However, this correlation varies significantly across studied models and between imgtxt vs. txtimg. For example, in UniAR the correlation is strongest for txtimg transfer (ρ = 0.76). In all three models the correlating direction is the one whose intra-modality steering is strongest (imgimg in UniAR, txttxt in Liquid and Emu3.5), i.e. where the denominator of the recovery ratio is reliable. Steering vectors show some alignment despite modality gap. For example, the happysad vectors found in text and in images point in somewhat similar directions, with cosine similarity of 0.47 in UniARs mid layers. Broadly, there could be two explanations for this: 1) The text and image activations for happy inputs are close, text and image activations for sad inputs are close, therefore the two difference vectors are close. 2) Text and image occupy separate subspaces but the two subspace share similar structure, i.e., relations between the activations in each space are similar. Setup: We test both explanations in UniARs representation space: each concept pole in each modality (e.g., happy images) is summarized by the mean activation over its minimal-pair examples. Activations are strongly anisotropic: two random activations of the same modality have cosine similarity of about 0.75 at the middle layers, and two from opposite modalities still 0.65. Therefore, we rescale them to unit length and subtract the overall mean before computing cosines (Appendix C); the steering vectors themselves are unaffected by this centering. We find evidence for the second explanation: Image and text occupy separate narrow spaces inside the model, while the relative directions between activations within each region exhibits some alignment. If the first explanation were right, happy image and happy sentence would sit close together in the model. However, in UniARs middle layers, the average happy image is more than ten times closer to the average sad image than to the average happy sentence, with similar or stronger trend 630 of the 42 (concept, layer range) points of UniAR and Liquid in Figure 5 lie more than two standard deviations (0.03) above random baseline. 8 Preprint. Under review. for every concept. On the other hand, the steering directions extracted in text and in images have cosine similarity between 0.14 and 0.60 for five of the eight concepts, far above random-direction baseline of 0.03, while size, near-far and spatial-lr are around zero. Emu3.5 and Liquid show the same separation by modality. Our findings illustrate that steering vectors can provide separate avenue for quantifying whether unified model is actually unified. Aligned directions despite separate subspaces is also related to modality-gap studies in contrastive embedding spaces (Liang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024) and the vector-offset regularities in word embeddings, i.e., the famous king-queen example (Mikolov et al., 2013b; Park et al., 2024) and the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (Huh et al., 2024; Groger et al., 2026).

sections.title: 4 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Unification and Alignment of Modalities. Approaches and tasks for connecting vision and language differ widely, from multimodal language models (Lu et al., 2019; Tsimpoukelli et al., 2021; Alayrac et al., 2022), text-conditioned image generation (Rombach et al., 2022), multimodal retrieval (Radford et al., 2021), to the many variants of recent unified multimodal models (Team, 2025; Wang et al., 2026b; Deng et al., 2025). Across all, it is widely studied how vision and language representations interact and align (Merullo et al., 2023; Neo et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025a), ranging from modality gaps studies in CLIP models (Liang et al., 2022) to circuit analyses and vocabulary space projections in multimodal LLMs (Nikankin et al., 2025; Krojer et al., 2026; Feucht et al., 2026). Only few works have studied internals of unified models, via attention patterns and embedding geometry Serra et al. (2025), transfer of knowledge edits Gao et al. (2026) and steering vectors Wang & Li (2026). They often report lack of unification (Serra et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2026), in contrast to our more positive findings. Most similar to us is Wang & Li (2026) who report cross-modal steering vectors in only one direction (txtimg). They primarily study different type of UMM, BAGEL (Deng et al., 2025) with separate language and image generation weights and objectives, while relying on minimal text inputs for both text and image vectors. Finally, they study closed-form QA text outputs and not our setting of free-form text. Visual steering. Most related to our transfer question, Gan et al. (2026) and Deng et al. (2026) each study one direction of transfer (text to image tokens and image to text, respectively) to alter the visual understanding of MLLMs, which only take images as conditioning. Other continuous attribute control in image generation (Baumann et al., 2025; Ekin & Gandelsman, 2026; Dalva & Yanardag, 2024; Kamenetsky et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026a) likewise targets diffusion models rather than the shared space of unified model. Steering the visual-token stream of an autoregressive image generator, as we do, is rarely explored (Chrabaszcz et al., 2026; Wang & Li, 2026). Textual steering. Identifying and applying linear and non-linear concept directions started with operating on embeddings themselves (Mikolov et al., 2013a; Bolukbasi et al., 2016). Now, we operate in the latent spaces of language models for both exact and attribute-based steering (Subramani et al., 2019; 2022; You et al., 2026). For these causal steering operations, data often comes from contrastive prompt pairs (Turner et al., 2024; Rimsky et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2025), in-context task demonstrations (Todd et al., 2024), or sparse-autoencoder features (Huben et al., 2024), all grounded in the linear representation hypothesis (Park et al., 2024).

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: In this paper we have shown cross-modal steering vectors in both directions (txtimg and imgtxt). We also characterized and provided intuition how such cross-modal steering can manifest in the other modality. As unified multimodal models become more capable and mature as field, we see potential for methods that leverage this unified nature for model control. If we identify promising (steering) intervention to make models safer (Arditi et al., 2024), it should automatically transfer to visual capabilities; likewise, if we want to regularly update knowledge in the model, such knowledge edits should transfer to visual capabilities (Gao et al., 2026). We encourage future work to expand our findings to other families of unified models and novel concepts. Scientifically, we see unified models as fruitful testbed for developing modality-agnostic interpretability tools and theories of multimodal interactions, as exemplified by our study of cross-modal steering. 9 Preprint. sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: Our work studies internal steering directions of open-weight unified multimodal models on synthetic minimal pairs; we foresee no direct ethical concerns beyond the plethora of general risks of controllable generation, including generation of harmful content targeting and/or exploiting vulnerable populations.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: the construction of the minAppendix contains everything needed to reproduce our results: imal pairs with all edit the evaluation prompts, decoding settings per model, instructions, layer and strength selection, the judge prompts and metrics, and the human validation. Appendix details the geometry analyses. Code is at https://github.com/saintsauceee/ cross-modal-steering, and the minimal pairs, steering vectors, generations and judge scores at https://huggingface.co/saintsauce.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: We used generative AI tools throughout this project, always in back-and-forth with the authors, and not simply adopting what they suggest. Research and experiments. We used coding agents to implement the methods and to run most experiments reported in the paper, including cleaning and reformatting the generated data. Some methodological decisions, the hypotheses we tested, and how prior work has approached the problem were also discussed with AI tools. We never blindly adopted their suggestions, it was long back-and-forth in which we often disagreed with the AI assistant and often stuck to our own scientific intuition. AI assistants also helped interpret results and describe qualitative patterns in steered outputs; every such interpretation was checked against the underlying numbers and generations by the authors. We did not review agent-written code line by line. Instead, we discussed the code and its outputs with the agent, re-ran experiments, and sanity-checked results (e.g., for strange or implausible values) before adopting them into the paper. Data and evaluation. We used generative AI models to automatically generate the minimal pairs for concept directions, including the French sentences of the language-identity pairs, and the evaluation prompts (Appendices A.1 and A.2). The authors inspected the generated pairs and measured how minimal they are before using them. An LLM (Gemini 3.7 Flash) served as the judge for all reported metrics; its agreement with human raters is reported in Appendix A.8. Writing, figures and literature. The final paper is the full responsibility of, and was primarily driven by, us authors. We sometimes adopted isolated sentence-level suggestions from AI assistants, especially for sentences reporting technical details or for rephrasing suboptimal phrase, and used them much more sparingly for writing than for coding and experiments. AI tools helped create the figures, and helped identify and summarize related work; when an AI tool suggested citations, we checked them against its original source. We did not use AI for developing theoretical models or for formulating or proving mathematical claims (not applicable here). All AI-assisted content was reviewed by the authors, who take responsibility for the final content of this work. Preprint. Under review.

sections.content: 19 32 38 40 46 Concepts. Our concepts are chosen from those commonly studied in either the language or vision community. Emotion (sad/happy) is commonly steered in language models (Turner et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2025), and age (young/old) and expression are canonical targets of latent-direction editing in image generation (Shen et al., 2020; Gandikota et al., 2024; Baumann et al., 2025). Cleanness and chaos are semantic concepts that describe the state of whole scene. In text single word expresses them, while in an image they are spread over many objects, which makes them an interesting test of whether one direction can capture both. The visual concepts describe basic properties of objects in scene, such as their size, depth, spatial position or color. We expect spatial (left/right) to be the hardest concept to steer, since spatial relations are well-documented failure mode of image generation models and VLMs (Chatterjee et al., 2024; Kamath et al., 2023). For people in the color concept, the template is {subject} is dressed in {pole}. Traditionally, steering operates on single layer, at one or all timesteps depending on the task (Subramani et al., 2022), but more recent work has found success steering multiple or even all layers (Zou et al., 2025; Gaintseva et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2025). Different layers encode different linguistic properties and later layers tend to encode more complex features in neural network models (Ethayarajh, 2019; Tenney et al., 2019; Rogers et al., 2020; Skean et al., 2025; Li & Subramani, 2026). We therefore compare early, middle and late layers without choosing one over the others.7 We steer seven layer configurations per model: three single layers, three contiguous layer ranges and all layers, listed in Table 5. sections.content: Judge. The judge is Gemini 3.7 Flash with low thinking level and one sample per comparison, and JSON response schema restricts its verdict to A, or Tie. It never sees any steering hyper7In interpretability, splitting layers into early, middle, and late is common practice (Subramani et al., 2026). 26 Preprint. Under review. parameter, such as α, the layer configuration or the steering vector. We validate it against human reviewers in Appendix A.8. Prompt. The prompts are shown below, where {pole} is the asked pole, {anchor} the opposite pole and {answer} the raters answer. We prompt the judge few-shot with ten example pairs for each modality. They are held-out pairs on which the reviewers agreed, and their answers are spread evenly across the steered output, the baseline and tie. The question names one of the two poles at random, so the judge cannot score well just by recognizing steering artifacts. Concept rate judge: image pair You are careful annotator comparing two model outputs. Here are examples of how this rater judges such pairs. shows numbered rows; in each row the left panel is and the right panel is B: The image Row 1: Answer: ... Which represents more of {pole} (or less of {anchor})? {answer} Row 10: Answer: Which represents more of {pole} (or less of {anchor})? {answer} [example grid image, rows 1A1B to 10A10B] Now judge this new pair the same way: A: [image A] B: [image B] Which represents more of {pole} (or less of {anchor})? Judge only the attribute - ignore style, grammar, and quality. candidate that looks odd, broken, or repetitive can still clearly show the attribute (e.g. it repeats the trait), and is not automatically Tie; decide only by whether the attribute itself is clearly stronger in one. Answer with one word (A, B, or Tie). 27 Preprint. Under review. Concept rate judge: text pair You are careful annotator comparing two model outputs. Here are examples of how this rater judges such pairs: [10 examples, in the format below] Now judge this pair the same way: Candidate A: [text A] Candidate B: [text B] Which represents more of {pole} (or less of {anchor})? Judge only the attribute - ignore style, grammar, and quality. candidate that looks odd, broken, or repetitive can still clearly show the attribute (e.g. it repeats the trait), and is not automatically Tie; decide only by whether the attribute itself is clearly stronger in one. Answer with one word (A, B, or Tie). Text example format Example: Candidate A: [example text A] Candidate B: [example text B] Which text represents more of {pole} (or less of {anchor})? Choose or B, or Tie if its not obvious. Answer with one word (A, B, or Tie). Answer: {answer} A.6 DREAMSIM POLE SCORE (IMAGES) As complement to the concept rate metric for images, we compare each generated image with two references, positive-pole and negative-pole edit of the same scene. With the cosine distance in DreamSim, learned perceptual image similarity (Fu et al., 2023), the pole score of an image with references R+, is pole(I) = 100 d(I, R) d(I, R+) + d(I, R) , so 100 means matches the positive-pole reference, 0 the negative-pole reference, and 50 is equidistant. The references for prompt are the models own unsteered image, minimally edited toward each pole with Gemini 3 Pro Image, following the same method as the minimal pairs. 28 Preprint. Under review. Figure 7 plots the pole score against normalized strength for the two image-output settings. It rises with α for the concepts that steer and stays flat at 50 for spatial. The same rise appears when text-derived vector steers image generation. Figure 7: DreamSim pole score for image-derived (left) and text-derived (right) vectors. UniAR moves the furthest, with age strongest and every concept except spatial rising, apart from size under the text-derived vector. In Emu3.5 and Liquid the shifts are only few points: color moves most with both vectors, and age moves mainly with the text-derived vector. In Liquid, size and depth sit above 50 at every strength without moving, so their offset is not steering. A.7 FLUENCY AND COHERENCE JUDGES Text. We use an AxBench-style pointwise fluency judge (Wu et al., 2025b). Gemini 3.7 Flash scores each output 0, 1 or 2 for fluency and sees only the output, never the prompt, the strength or the layer. We score all 22,400 steered text outputs per model plus one unsteered baseline per concept and prompt. The prompt is shown below. 29 Preprint. Under review. Text fluency You are evaluating the linguistic fluency of language model output. Model output: {text} Rate the fluency and coherence of the output. Use the following scale: 0 = The output is substantially incoherent, ungrammatical, or otherwise difficult to understand. 1 = The output is understandable but contains noticeable issues with grammar, coherence, or naturalness. 2 = The output is fluent, coherent, grammatical, and natural. Focus only on linguistic quality. Do not judge whether the output follows the original instruction or expresses the target concept. Return JSON only: {"score": 0 1 2, "reasoning": "<one concise sentence>"} Images. For images we build the counterpart of the fluency judge: the same model sees only the image, with no prompt, concept or strength, and returns one of three verdicts, intact, partly broken or broken, which we map to 2/1/0. We use verdict words rather than numeric scale, which returned 1 for nearly every image. We score all 3,200 steered images per model at the middle layer range and the 160 unsteered baselines. The prompt is shown below. Image coherence You are checking an image generated by model for visible breakage. Answer with one of three verdicts: "intact": the image is coherent and well-formed. This is the expected verdict for typical generated image; the usual look of AI-generated images (smoothness, softness, synthetic feel) is not breakage. "partly_broken": the content is recognizable, but there are clear artifacts, distortions, or incoherent elements, such as malformed hands or faces, merged or duplicated objects, garbled text, or corrupted regions. "broken": severe artifacts or garbled textures dominate, or the content cannot be recognized. Only visible breakage matters. Do not judge whether the image matches any description or expresses any concept, and do not judge style, aesthetics, or realism. Return JSON only: {"reasoning": "<one concise sentence naming any breakage you see, or stating that there is none>", "verdict": "intact" "partly_broken" "broken"} Results. Figure 8 plots both quality scores next to the concept rate against normalized strength, each relative to the models unsteered outputs. Text fluency holds up to about 0.4 of the range, where the concept rate peaks, and collapses beyond it. Image coherence declines gently over the 30 Preprint. Under review. whole range while the concept rate keeps rising. Transferred and intra-modality vectors degrade quality similarly, except that image-derived vectors cost text fluency more than text-derived ones in Emu3.5 and Liquid at middle strengths. Quality is text fluency (left) and image coherence (right), relative to the unsteered outputs. A.8 HUMAN VALIDATION To check that the automated concept-rate judge tracks human judgment, we collect human annotations on 320 held-out pairs, 10 per concept and setting across eight concepts, none of which is part of the evaluated sweeps. Each pair receives three independent reviews. Reviewers face the same forced-choice task as the judge: the steered output and its α = 0 baseline shown as and in randomized order, with the asked pole also randomized (50% the steered pole, 50% the opposite), and are blind to α, the layer, and which output is steered. Figure 9 shows the annotation interface. 31 Preprint. Under review. Figure 9: The annotation interface shown to human reviewers. It names the asked pole and its opposite. Two model outputs, the unsteered baseline and the steered output, are shown as Candidate and in random order. The human reviewer answers A, or Tie. Since the A/B order and the asked pole are random, we recode each answer as agreeing with the steering direction, going against it, or tie, and combine the three reviews of pair by majority vote, breaking three-way splits at random. Cohens κ between the judge and this majority label is 0.62 over the 320 pairs.

sections.title: F BEHIND THE SCENES
sections.content: The goal of this section is to show the behind the scenes beyond the final polished paper: Why we started working on this, all the detours and failures, and what lessons we learned. It is meant to make science more fun, transparent and accessible to newcomers8. We show both DZs side of the story, i.e., the first author, and also BKs side as the last author. F.

sections.title: JUNIOR PERSPECTIVE
sections.content: How it started. This project was my first real experience doing research. It grew out of personal interest in vision-language models (VLMs), following natural language understanding course project in which we studied their behaviour on spatial reasoning tasks. Over time, found myself reading more about new ideas for visual reasoning, reasoning in general, and various other topics that caught my attention. Eventually, came across mechanistic interpretability and began exploring model internals. was particularly fascinated by the residual stream and the idea that we could look beyond models outputs to investigate how information is represented and processed within it. At that point, had no research question in mind, just an interest in low-level understanding of these models. Interpretability looks cool. started digging deeper into interpretability, exploring work on model circuits, activation patching, causal tracing, superposition, and sparse autoencoders. spent quite some time reading on these ideas and began exchanging thoughts and discussing possible project ideas with Benno, who would supervise the research. We explored an initial direction with activation patching, but it never quite developed into something we were satisfied with. Benno then suggested activation steering, which offered simple, practical, and would argue, elegant way to intervene in models internal representations and observe how its behavior changed. Humble beginnings. Our first candidate was Metas Chameleon, which seemed almost ideal on paper: simple, unified architecture with decent image generation capabilities. Unfortunately, its image generation components were not publicly released. We then considered alternatives such as Anole, but the additional training required was beyond our commitment budget. Eventually, we settled on Janus, and later UniToken, which finally allowed us to start experimenting. Early results were fairly encouraging for few concepts, which became our go-to smoke tests for subsequent experiments. However, image generation was strong limitation, with distorted faces and various other visual artifacts. These models were useful for testing our ideas, but their image generation quality made it hard to rigorously draw meaningful conclusions or properly support our main research question. Tough luck. Alongside our main model, UniAR, we also experimented with Bagel, arguably one of the strongest and more well-known open-source unified multimodal models. Its image generation capabilities were impressive (e.g., very pretty images), but its diffusion-based image generation introduced lot of complexity. Additionally, although its pre-training was strongly unified, we werent entirely sure how unified the model itself really was. This led to many discussions about whether it was appropriate for addressing our main research question. The right fit. Model selection remained one of the biggest challenges throughout the project. Although we wanted to answer broader questions about how vision and language interact within multimodal models, we were quite particular about the models we used. We specifically wanted unified models in which both modalities are processed within shared architecture rather than studying cross-modal interactions through separate components. However, finding model that was sufficiently unified while also having strong image generation capabilities turned out to be surprisingly difficult. One day, while scrolling through Rednote (a social media platform), came across post showing the UniAR paper from the Qwen team and Fudan University. After discussing it with Benno, we quickly moved on to our usual smoke tests, and the results looked very interesting. Surprisingly, even some concepts that hadnt worked at all with previous models, such as depth near/far, showed encouraging results. The image generation quality was, overall, decently impressive (the generated images were very pretty). After all of it, UniAR finally seemed to be what we had been looking for. 8bennokrojer.com/behind-the-scenes 47 Preprint. Under review. The bigger picture. Throughout the project, my discussions with Benno, particularly his interest in more fundamental scientific questions, gradually changed how looked at our work and inspired me to be more curious. Initially, it felt like series of experiments on manipulating model behavior. It then became: how do vision and language interact, to what extent do they share common understanding of the world, and more. After Tamar and Nishant joined the project, also had the chance to witness great minds debate novel ideas, navigate through ambiguity in strong, systematic way, and develop creative yet rigorous ways to test new hypotheses. hope our work can serve as useful starting point for studying cross-modal behaviour. Beyond demonstrating where concrete cross-modal steering methods succeed or fail, hope our findings can help others better understand and study the relationship between visual and linguistic representations. There are still so many abstract ideas, but think that is precisely what makes this direction worth exploring! F.2 SENIOR PERSPECTIVE This project was unique because it was DZs first time doing research and BKs first time fully supervising an undergraduate end-to-end, from ideation to our final submission. BK had mentored undergraduates before but in those cases the student either had already some experience and direction in mind or it did not end up as final conference submission. So, this mentoring from blank slate to full conference submission was proud moment! The project itself. When DZ approached me for an independent study at McGill, the ideas were still broadly around visual concepts in models. There was lot of motivation and curiosity but lot of scoping to be done. So we brainstormed for few weeks and, while dont remember how exactly, eventually we stumbled upon the idea of transferring steering vectors across modalities. thought this would be very elegant and novel to study, and probably under-explored. More broadly had been waiting for chance to do interpretability on unified multimodal models, as opposed to the more mainstream VLMs. So the project properly took this shape around late January 2026, and then as DZ describes above, it was many-months journey of finding the right models to study. The lesson here is that for lot of interesting phenomena, one has to wait for the right moment, such as model capabilities or architectures to mature. In our case models had to get bit better at generating images perhaps, especially fully autoregressive unified models. UniAR is relatively unknown and new model but came at the right time for us (Peng et al., 2026). Thoughts on modality unification. It is unclear if we are close to reaching the grand goal that made researchers develop unified multimodal models in the first place. Intuitively, there should be lots of synergies and overlaps between visual and textual capabilities. Therefore, the goal is broadly that we want single model that can generate anything from the same underlying representation space. However from the capabilities angle, these models have not really replaced mainstream LLaVA-style VLMs or diffusion-based text-to-image models. And from an analysis angle, there has been some early evidence that these unified models might not actually be particularly unified internally (Serra et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2026). One also has to simply acknowledge that the design space here is much vaster and trickier than for pure text or image generation (Tong et al., 2026). So while analysis work on earlier unified models might have shown mostly negative results, newer models, with years of engineering insights baked into them, might be much more unified. But for the next couple years, am still not too optimistic about this line of work. For example, interpretability studies on unified models might still be considered less mainstream or impactful. But long-term there is still optimism that these models will become the mainstream paradigm, since they follow the spirit that has dominated AI development in the last decade: Instead of designing different models for different tasks or domains, build one general model. This will then open up exciting and difficult challenges for interpretability and cognitive science, such as much more interesting questions about acquisition during pre-training. For someone considering working on them from this analysis angle, would recommend to go for it but to be aware that this field might not be the most impactful or trendy for while. Reflections on mentoring, becoming senior researcher and beyond. Some of this project was completed at the end of BKs PhD and some during the newly started postdoc. It therefore represents very well the transition from being hands-on PhD student to more senior role of mentorship and 48 Preprint. Under review. supervision. Such transition is not easy and requires very different skills than those needed for hands-on leading project. So just like DZ, BK also learned lot. Some reflections on the different kind of skills this senior role brings forth, compared to the usual skills acquired during the first years of PhD: 1. After being used to having control over every aspect of the project as PhD student, it will not be easy to let go of such control and trust the student and the process. 2. On the other hand, it is equally important to know when to take over from the student. This is especially true for writing where it is unrealistic to expect an undergraduate to know all the unspoken rules and nuances of conference submission paper. So BK ended up framing or writing large chunks of the paper based on DZs initial results and drafts, and with help from the other two senior authors. 3. It is also not an easy balance what kind of Claude Code habits to recommend, such that the student still learns by themselves mostly. 4. There is not single best way of mentoring so adding few other more senior roles was very helpful, both for me to refine my ideas with another senior person, and for DZ to witness different approaches to science, project habits and paper writing. It is very useful skill to know who could be good additions to project, especially when there is no actual PI on the project. Even when you are not yet close to finishing your PhD, highly recommend mentoring undergrads. But also recommend being realistic about it. Do not pour your hopes into the project immediately, expecting them to be like mini-PhD student from day one. Instead, the more you see evidence of scientific curiosity, self-initiative and long-term commitment, the more you can gradually increase your expectations and time investment. The beautiful part of such experiences is how it re-connects you with the younger version of yourself when you entered research, perhaps naive but also full of excitement and energy. It teaches empathy and lets you see the process of science from birdseye-view: never-ending cycle of standing on the shoulders of giants, of continuous mentoring and nurturing spirit of exploration.
